chapter: U Street, Jelly Roll Morton, the youth band and the WPA
title: Fired over Don Redman's Chant of the Weed, then learning the whole show at home
summary: The chordless, advanced score defeats him and the owner lets him go; he buys the show's music and teaches himself, setting a lifelong habit.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: So when the time came for rehearsal, the first piece they passed out was a piece called .. It was a dance number, and it was a piece written by Don Redman that they used as a theme song. It was called "Chant of the Weed." So the bandleader handed this piece of music to me which seemed to stretch all the way across the piano. And I looked at it, and there was
not a chord on it anywhere. There were chords, but the chords were all written; there were no chord symbols there.

"The Chant of the Weed" was a piece that was far ahead of its time. When I hear it now, I realize that it had... I don't remember, but I know it had things like augmented elevenths and thirteenth chords and all that in it, which I hadn't ever played and had seldom even heard any chord... The only time I had ever heard a chord that sounded that way was maybe one that Duke Ellington might have ended a tune on. But to hear these chords consecutively behind one another, in one piece, just blew my mind. I didn't even know how to find it on a piano, because by that time I hadn't played anything beyond a ninth chord.
Anyway, I sat up there, and after two or three...

After two or three false starts on this piece... As I said, the music stretched across the piano, and I don't think I ever got out of the first 4 bars. The guy stopped the band and went over and talked to the club owner. And the club owner came over to me and said he wanted to talk to me. He took me in his office and he said, 'Son, you're a nice kid, a nice boy and everything, but I think that this is a little bit

too..." He didn't say "too heavy," but the expression meant the same thing. "I don't think you can do this. This is a little bit too much for you." I made some feeble attempt at trying to tell him that if I had a chance, that I could learn it or something. He said, "Well, we don't have time for anything like that. This show opens tonight. We haven't gotten out of the first number, and the show is an hour-and-a-half long."

So I told him, "Okay." He thanked me, and I went on out with tears coming down my cheeks! But I got home, and I got to thinking about it, and I remembered the name of this thing -- and I went and I bought music to everything I could find in that show. As a matter, I think I had a list that they had given me of the rundown. I took all this music home, and that became my lesson! I would study it, you know. And after learning it, I felt like I had learned a hell of a lot just by learning that. Then that set a precedent, because after that, up until now, anything that I run up against that's rough musically, I take it home and learn it. And I think any musician, if he does that, you'll always go ahead. So it was just one of those things that...
